utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened, Madam Registrar? Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Appearances Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman, with David Cunningham, and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you too. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour. Can I re-emphasise what Mr. Nicholls raised at the end of yesterday's session that we would like to tomorrow before we break the running order of the witnesses between the 26th of November and Christmas, please. The reason I ask for it is as was explained yesterday, we do have to prioritise the work, and unless we know who is coming, we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have the list of all the witnesses we are going to call by the end of December. In the Prosecution case, we had to prioritise our work and we had to prepare, and they wouldn't give us that kind of information until the Thursday before the next week. That was the rule. That's the rule we want to follow. I think it's fair. If they did it that way, we get to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not in fact right as I've explained over and over again. Your Honour, the thing is Mr. Ackerman has put back now a whole series of witnesses, and we don't know whether they're coming before Christmas or what order they're coming. So, Your Honour, I don't think it's an unreasonable request, and I certainly don't think it's an unreasonable request to know who is coming on the week of the 26th and the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I mean, let's not waste time on these matters. The case of the Prosecution was somewhat different in the sense that we were dealing with municipality after municipality, which is not the case in your case. You've given an initial list of witnesses, which has basically been divided into two parts. One part that you seem to be in a position to bring forward until you finish your case as promised at the end of January. And another list which we don't, but we accept your word, that it's not likely that these people will be called. January is January, and November and December is a different period of time. What is being asked is since we are stopping now, and you have been shifting more or less the position of these witnesses as we went along, and I think the Prosecution at least ought to be put in a position of -- we're talking of two weeks basically, two weeks, three weeks. Whether we can stick to the list of witnesses that we have shown for the weeks starting 1st December, 8 December, 15th December, and 25th, which now 26th November.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I point out, if you have the list, the two witnesses who were due to testify this week aren't testifying. The two witnesses who were supposed to testify on the 25th of November are now testifying this week. So I would like to know, please, for the week of what's now the 26th of November, are we having the two witnesses who should have been called on the 10th of November or are we working to the 1st of December or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when I made this request in the Prosecution case, it was an unreasonable request and Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not argue. Even we want to know what the position is because the two witnesses we are having this week weren't supposed to be testifying this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, if you order me to provide it by tomorrow, I'll do that. I just think it's unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why do I get treated differently than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not being treated differently. You are just shifting the order of the witnesses from one week to the next. And you've been doing it practically since we started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did they.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And understand that logistically it may become necessary and you haven't been doing capriciously, but on the other hand, they ought to know and we ought to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge very frequently, we found out on Thursday who the witness was going to be on Monday. They wouldn't tell us before that. That's true. That's what happened. Now you're making me do something totally different, and it's just not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is coming over the week of the 26th, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I said I would provide it tomorrow if you order me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start from there. So the witness now. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want the record to show that I complained more than once that we were not getting information until the Thursday before We only had a few days to prepare cross-examination for the Monday witness. You've never ordered them to do it any differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I have them all, and I will produce them to you if you need them, but we have had lists months ahead of all the witnesses that the Prosecution was going to produce, say, in Sanski Most or in Kljuc or whatever. And then practically most of the time, Prosecution stuck to the order in which that list was shown. It's true that it was confirmed on the Thursday before, but you had the list before, and the practice was to stick to that list and the order, with the exception of when witnesses weren't called or when they -- there was some problem, which I anticipate will occur also in your case. But it's just sense of cooperation. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have another matter to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm becoming concerned about the length of time that's being consumed with regard to these witnesses. And I'm mostly concerned about that consumption of time which involves nothing more than showing a witness an exhibit and having the witness confirm that it says what it says for the sole purpose of having Your Honours look at the exhibit again. And I'm as guilty of it as anyone. I've done it. And if we're going to be able to put on in the short time we have been allowed the number of witnesses we need to put on, we need to find a way to shorten this process up. So what I strongly suggest is that you not permit any of us to use an exhibit with a witness unless the witness is familiar with that document and can make some contribution to the Trial Chamber's understanding of that document or its contents. But just to show the witness a document so that you all will see it again for maybe the fourth or fifth time makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, before I even ask Ms. Korner because what you are saying has been in the back of my mind for quite some time. We do lose time when it comes to showing witnesses documents. But I strongly disagree with something that you have just said, that it should become the rule not to show the witness documents with which he or she may not be familiar. First of all, how are we supposed to know whether the witness is familiar with a particular document or not? That's number one. So you can only find that out if you show the witness the document. And secondly, I disagree also with you that a witness would not be in a position to enlighten the Chamber or to give information on a document with which he or she is not familiar. We have had -- we have had many witnesses being shown documents which then they read, and all of a sudden, I mean, it dawned on them why certain things happened, why certain decisions were implemented and so -- I mean, I agree with you that we should be practical and reduce as much as possible the time taken first in locating these documents, and then showing them to the witness. That is time consuming. I agree with you. And if we can find a solution, which I can only see if these documents are prepared beforehand by whoever intends to make use of them and by the Registrar in particular, that's the only way. Then I don't know if you have other suggestions. Please come forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is, of course, and let's take Mr. Radic, he wouldn't take a thing unless he saw a document. I am equally happy not to have to put documents because of the time it takes, and I have been very guilty of not marking up the B/C/S version. In future, if I show documents they will be marked for the witness if it's more difficult to find. But it seems to me that you can't say if a witness says "show me the document" I refuse. So that's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely not. It's out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I point out that yesterday we sat for 45 minutes because Mr. Ackerman's next witness wasn't here. It seems to me that it's better in the interests of not wasting time that Mr. Ackerman has witnesses here even if they have to wait. So -- but Your Honour, I'm happy to simply not put documents and say, Mr. X, there's a document, I'm not going to show it to you, but take it from me it says this. I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, let's close this chapter down. I appeal to you to make minimal use of documents only when it's necessary. And to have them ready. I know that you have assistants, and the more or less you are prepared beforehand. What I would also kindly ask you to do is to make sure that the Registrar is also in possession of the list of the documents you entered, and that they have them ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we give them the list. We can't make sure they get the documents ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, that's not your problem. But what I'm inviting the Registrar to do is to have these documents ready. Perhaps after consulting with the party producing those documents, whether they will be made use of or not. Because most of the time, I notice that there's a whole list of documents, of exhibits, that purportedly are intended to be made use of, and then maybe 10 per cent of them. And I can also understand that that happens as you go along with the questioning because some documents are in the list because you don't know what question to expect, what answer to expect to a particular question. So I do understand that. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other reason is there's an objection if we produce a document that's not on the list. So it's better in our estimation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it has been done all the time. We complain if it's not on the list because usually we don't have it. But it could be dug up straight away by Madam Registrar and put on the ELMO. We have got all that facility. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just two very brief things, with regard to the handling of documents, we have adopted a whole new strategy in that regard. We won't require the Registrar to pull one document, I don't think, during this direct examination. Everything will be on Sanction or there's a book prepared for the witness with the B/C/S with the portions highlighted. So there shouldn't have to be one document pulled, we hope, and that should speed things up dramatically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you continue with this efficiency, Mr. Ackerman, you will be tempted to join the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This witness must absolutely be out of here tomorrow. So I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not sitting on Friday anyway. So it's in everybody's interest to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I will finish my direct today and I expect Ms. Korner will finish her cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the reason Mr. Ackerman is raising that is cause I raised with him this yesterday that this was clearly an important witness. That's my complaint - my complaint - about not sitting on Tuesday. That witness had he been brought up could have started. Your Honour, I don't know what he's going to say, but the summary says he's going to talk about the background to the Serbs walking out of the assembly. He can discuss the formation of the SDS party Kljuc, how it was formed, provocation, he can discuss events in the national assembly. Your Honour, I will do my best, but if he's going to cover everything that's in that summary, well then, Your Honour, he may be allowed to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start and see what the position will be. There are no protective measures? So Madam usher, could you bring Mr. Kalabic in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. I take it that you are receiving interpretation in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to give evidence as a witness brought forward, produced by the accused in this case, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Our rules require that before you start your testimony, you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing put the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath, and it is an undertaking on your part. Madam usher is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out loud, and that will be your commitment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair. I'll explain very briefly what's going to happen. You are a witness for the Defence, and therefore who is going to question you first is Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for the accused Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman will then be followed by Ms. Korner who is the lead counsel for the Prosecutor in this case, and she'll cross-examine you. On the basis of the oath that you have just taken, your duty here is to answer each and every question truthfully and fully without any mental reservations and without omitting to say what you know. Your duty also does not depend on who is asking you the question. You do not have a right to distinguish between questions put to you by Mr. Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin or questions forthcoming from the Prosecution. Your duty is only towards the truth. And therefore you have -- you're bound by law to answer each question truthfully and fully. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Rajko Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you give the Chamber just a sort of brief educational background, places you went to school, degrees you achieved, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I completed primary and secondary school in Kljuc in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then I went to the faculty of forestry in Sarajevo where I graduated. I worked in Kljuc as an engineer, and I was politically active as an assemblyman in the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of parliament. After the end of the war, I stopped being politically active and started working as a private businessman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political parties?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party from 1990. Up to then, I had been a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, or rather, of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been involved in politics up until now?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Most of the questions I'm going to be asking you deal with the period of time 1991, 1992, and maybe a tiny bit of 1993. So that will be the context in which I will ask you questions. The first question I want to ask you is if you knew or you knew of a Professor Muhamed Filipovic from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew of Professor Muhamed Filipovic. I heard about him, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a book prepared that the usher will give you that has in it all of the exhibits that I'll be asking you to take a look at. It has numbered tabs, and I'll tell you each time which numbered tab to look under. I'm wondering if you recall Professor Muhamed Filipovic visiting Kljuc in the summer of 1991 and making a speech there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember Mr. Filipovic's visit to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit P854. It's tab 1 in your book. And you should see highlighted there some parts of that document that I'm interested in having you look at. And it's things that Professor Filipovic said at the speech. And I just want to ask you about some of them. The first part says that he first addressed the people of Kljuc, pointing out that it was a place where he felt at ease, where there are no ethnic clashes because the lessons of the past have been learned well and where people respect each other and that it should stay that way. Was that, in fact, the situation that existed in Kljuc in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, this was the situation in Kljuc. It was peaceful. There were no interethnic clashes or tensions. And this went on. In the past, because Mr. Filipovic referred to the past, since he knew that in the past, in 1941, there was a horrific pogrom of the Serbian people where over a thousand people - exclusively Serbs - were killed and buried in a cemetery near Kljuc. A monument was erected there, and from time to time memorial ceremonies were held there on the anniversary of this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, we'll talk about that in a few minutes. The next thing I want to point out to you and ask you about that was said by Professor Filipovic was this. He was speaking of the three national parties, presumably SDS, SDA, and HDZ. And he said this: "In their seven months of rule, all the three national parties have to show is seeking weapons on all sides, log barricades, separatists, demonstrations of power. Instead of agreeing on a political program, the three parties have only agreed on a division of power." Do you agree with his analysis of what had happened during the seven months of the existence of these three national parties being in power?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I think in essence, this was not the case. Mr. Filipovic was one of the founders of the SDA party, together with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. But they parted ways politically, and Mr. Filipovic established a new Muslim party called the Muslim Bosniak Organisation. Of course, Mr. Filipovic was trying to make room for his party so that it could participate in the government and in the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslim Bosniak party had only two members of parliament. This was probably an effort to find a stronger base so as to be more influential in the government. As for his mentioning logs, separatists, and so on, he was probably alluding to the events in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those kinds of things hadn't started happening yet in Bosnia, and certainly not in the Kljuc area. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Kljuc area, nothing like that had happened. Everything was peaceful. People went to work normally. They worked as usual, and interethnic relations were quite normal. This speech was seen as referring to something that was not usual in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, I want to ask you about this other thing that he said here. "Slovenia's and Croatia's decision to secede from Yugoslavia will only make the situation more complicated for all, and particularly for Bosnia and Herzegovina, which cannot consent to agreements like the one between Cvetkovic and Macek, and the way they are making arrangements with - something - where Muslims would be a minority in a rump Yugoslavia and we do not want to live in this kind of Yugoslavia." In other words, he's saying that the Muslims don't want to be in a government where they would be in the minority. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: That's what was said. The secession of Slovenia and Croatia from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia complicated things in those areas. And it brought and instilled certain fear amongst everybody, amongst Muslims. There was indeed fear that they might be a national minority in the rump Yugoslavia if that rump Yugoslavia continued to exist as a rump Yugoslavia. On the other hand, the Serb people were also afraid that if Yugoslavia disappeared and if a centralised unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed, they would become a national minority. And going back to the developments and events in -- which took place in 1941, they were afraid that a similar thing might happen to them. So there was fear on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document, then. Let me ask you if you know and if you knew at the time another Muhamed Filipovic who lived and lives in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew a Muhamed Filipovic who was younger, who was a native of Kljuc, and who still lives in Kljuc to this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume you also knew his brother Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Omer Filipovic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, talking about this period of time in 1991, late 1991 when Professor Muhamed Filipovic came and the months after that, do you know what the relationships were like between Muhamed and Omer Filipovic and the members of the SDS, the Serbs, in Kljuc? Was the relationship comfortable? Was it uncomfortable? How was it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The relationship was normal. There were no tensions. People met each other. They talked to each other. So what I would say about that relationship is that it was normal at that time. Although I must also say that Omer Filipovic already at that time started delivering speeches which may have instigated and instilled fear amongst both ethnic groups. Muslims were being given to believe that something bad might happen to them. On the other hand, the Serbs were also given to believe that bad things might be done by the Muslims in the territory of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the talk was starting toward the end of 1991, the talk that was engendering fear. And wait until I tell you to go to the next document before you go. Let's finish up with this one first. What I said is correct. Right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Chamber just very briefly about the outcome of the multiparty elections in Kljuc and how the municipality was organised, who got various offices and things like that. And please do that as briefly as you can because the Chamber has heard it before, but I just want to set the scene a little bit for the rest of the questions I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The multiparty elections took place in 1990. There were several parties running for offices. The majority of the seats in the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc was won by the Serbian Democratic Party, followed by the SDA. And the Muslim Bosniak Organisation won two seats in the municipality. Nijaz Durakovic's party, the SDP - I don't know what the full name of this party is - also won two seats. Mr. Ante Markovic's party also had two or three seats. But the majority of the seats was won by the Serbian Democratic Party, followed by the SDA. The SDA and the Muslim Bosniak Organisation talked about a division of power, and they made a joint appearance in these talks. At the beginning, we agreed that the Serbian Democratic Party would be given three key positions in the municipality, and that the Muslim bloc would also be given three key positions in the municipality. The first position in the municipality at the time was the president of the municipal assembly. And this was given to the Serbian Democratic Party. The president of the municipal assembly was Mr. Jovo Banjac. His deputy was somebody from the Muslim bloc. That was Mr. Omer Filipovic. The second most important figure was the president of the executive board, and the person appointed to that position was from the Muslim bloc, Mr. Asim Egrlic. His deputy was a member of the SDS, Mr. Tihomir Dakic. The secretary of the municipal assembly, that is the person who worked along with the president of the municipal assembly and his deputy was a member of the SDS. At the beginning it was Vinko Kondic. And then he was replaced by Jovo Malbesa. The third position in the executive board was allocated to the Muslim bloc, and the person that was appointed was Fikret Balagic. So these were the six first and key positions in the municipality, and they were distributed in this manner despite the fact that the Serbian Democratic Party had the majority of the seats in the municipal assembly. In the secretariat for National Defence, the key position was given to the Serbian Democratic Party. That is to their representative, Slobodan Jurisic. The secretariat for general and legal affairs was given to the Muslim bloc, and the person appointed to the position of secretary was Merima Filipovic, the wife of Mr. Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if -- I leave it entirely up to you because your question asked for a brief description of the scene, portrayal of the scene. I leave it up to you whether you consider that brief or not. So please, take the witness completely under your control when you think he has gone beyond what you're seeking to obtain from him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to stop him myself because basically I think the information that he was giving was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But for the rest, I leave him in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I considered that a brief response, Your Honour, because it covered exactly what needed to be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, there's a document in tab 3 that I would now like you to look at. And this document is about a celebration of the anniversary of the SDS and a commemoration of the victims of the Ustasha genocide apparently held on the 28th or 29th of September 1991. My first question about this document is why --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's P861.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is why was there a commemoration in September of 1991 of the victims of Ustasha genocide? Why was that happening?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: This commemoration was organised to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the event that took place in 1941 when over a thousand Serb civilians were executed by the fascist forces. They were all buried in a joint grave in the territory of Kljuc. A monument was erected there for all the victims. So this was the 50th anniversary of this incident. However, this was not the only commemoration. Not only that year was a commemoration held. Such a commemoration was held every year. Wreaths would be placed at the monument for years. Every year there would be a memorial service. However, during those early years, we couldn't use the word "Ustasha genocide," but "fascist genocide," and we did not mention the real victims, their names or their ethnic origin. It was only this year, in 1991, when the spade was called a spade. So the genocide was mentioned as being an Ustasha genocide, and the victims were named as being Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you spoke at this memorial. And it should be highlighted there in your document. It says this: "Another speaker to address the assembly, Rajko Kalabic, SDS deputy from Kljuc, and a member of the Chamber of Municipalities in the BH Assembly, noted that this was the first occasion after World War II when we were actually reminded of the genocide which the Ustashas committed against the Serbian people. Rather late, but still in time to prevent history from repeating itself in its most horrible form. A foul war was being waged in one part of the country typified by the unleashing of a genocidal fascist hysteria on the part of the hordes controlled by and serving the goals of the pro-fascist and pro-Ustasha newly elected Croatian government." When you said in there that this was the first occasion after World War II when you were actually reminded of the genocide, what was the occasion that triggered that memory? What were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. What occasion are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in that -- the document at least quotes you of saying that you noted that this was the first occasion after World War II when we were actually reminded of the genocide. And I'm wondering what you meant by that? What was the first occasion that you were actually reminded? What are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: This was the first opportunity for the newly elected multiparty government after the socialist times in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina to speak more realistically of what really happened in 1941, who the victims were, who the perpetrators were, and what is happening again. And are the things that are happening again something that would remind us of the things that happened before in 1941?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "what's happening again," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: What I meant at that time was the breakup of Yugoslavia, the developments in the then Republic of Croatia. The war had already started in Croatia, and Serbs were already finding themselves on a different side, again being victims, having to leave their homes. Refugees were arriving in Kljuc and all this reminded us of the things that were happening in 1941 in Kljuc, and we were afraid that history could repeat itself again in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at another part now where you also made a statement. According to this document, you said the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the number of that document, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the same document, P861, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Why did they have this attitude towards the JNA, wondered Rajko Kalabic. And offered an answer: It was because they identified the JNA with a Serbian army, but it was wrong. The army was not just a Serbian army but the JNA in which all nations and nationalities were represented and which was fighting for the federal state." Now, stopping there, when you say "why did they have this attitude towards the JNA," who are you referring to? Who's "the they"?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: A certain number of people who were reserve officers of the JNA refused to respond to the mobilisation calls and join the ranks of the JNA. And that is why in my speech I alluded to them. In the former times, the reserve officers of the JNA would often go for manoeuvres and training. And whenever they went, they would be paid quite a lot of money. However, when the time came for us to preserve peace, Yugoslavia, and the JNA, then some of these people behaved differently and refused to join the ranks of the JNA. Not all of them, a few of them acted that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the JNA being composed of all nations and nationalities. Was that the case in September of 1991, October of 1991 when you made this talk?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case at the time. There were some people who refused to join the ranks of the JNA. At that time, JNA composed of Serbs and Croats. Truth be told, Croats had already left the JNA in Croatia. But in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were Croats in the JNA. There were Muslims, Macedonians, Serbians and so on and so forth. So JNA was still, for the most part, composed of all the ethnic groups, all the nationalities and national minorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then finally you talk about the creation of six national states in Yugoslavia, and you say that it's not satisfactory for the peoples living in Bosnia. You say that "only Yugoslavia could keep Bosnia-Herzegovina indivisible, not rifles, tanks, or the sacrifice of human life because it could be preserved only as a federal unit of a federative federal state. Everyone must help create a positive atmosphere, in particular those who worked in the public sector, party leaders, and manager, all citizens. Local media should also help to create this atmosphere." What are you asking for there? What is that plea?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind was the following: If peace is not sacrificed for the sovereignty of any of the republics of the former socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia, so if we sit down, if we talk, if we try and agree on things, if all the political figures, all the people in high positions, if they sit down and discuss things and reach an agreement, then there is a chance for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain integral. However, I was convinced that something like that is only possible in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Otherwise, I thought that the unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina could not guarantee the well being of the Serbian people. That is why I said that in order to have an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have to preserve a certain form of Yugoslavia. Maybe not with Croatia, maybe not with Slovenia. But some sort of Yugoslavia can guarantee peace and the integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll go to another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the information of the Chamber, and perhaps for the Prosecutor, the exhibit number is always displayed down in kind of the lower left-hand part of the screen, the second box on the left. You'll see P861 there. So you can always glean the exhibit number by looking there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The other thing, though, is that as Mr. Ackerman keeps pointing out, unless he mentions the name of the exhibit number, it doesn't go on the transcripts. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is P1139, and it's your tab 4, sir. This is a meeting of the executive committee of the Kljuc SDS held at 1700 hours on 2 October 1991 on the SDS premises. I'm showing you this document because your name appears in it. And you see that Krstan Zoric says: "I wish to thank Veljko Kondic and Rajko Kalabic for the speech they made because it was good." Do you know what speech he's referring to there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Kondic and Mr. Zoric had in mind my speech to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the pogrom of the Serbian people in Kljuc. And not only Mr. Kondic and Mr. Zoric. All those who wanted to voice their opinion could do so. And there were people who voiced their opinions and Krstan Zoric is the only one mentioned in the minutes who found it appropriate to say something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look a little further ahead in the document, you'll see a speech by Vinko Kondic. And just quickly tell the Chamber what his position was. Who was Vinko Kondic at this point?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was still the secretary of the municipal assembly. No, I apologise. Let me just try and remember. Later on, he was appointed chief of the public security station, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. He says -- he says in this meeting: "I don't expect the situation to improve. I don't think there will be a conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims, but I believe they are better organised than we are." Was that a general feeling at the time? Was it the general feeling that there was not going to be a conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the territory of Kljuc, that was the general feeling. Nothing pointed to the fact that the worst might happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, several people, then, had something to say. Vaso Stojanovic talked about there being a shortage of weapons, that he's afraid that younger men will leave and the old and infirm will remain unprotected and asked about the chances of obtaining weapons and distributing them to the people. Smiljanic talked about ambiguities about the army, that Uzelac should be supported. Zoric says there's a lot of fear among our people. It's important to know who remains in the village. And then finally Veljko Kondic says: "The fear is quite justified. The peace in Bosnia is being kept by a balance of fear." There's a lot of talk there about fear. What was the fear situation at this time in the Kljuc area? Was there a great deal of fear among the people?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Was there a great deal of fear? I can't confirm whether this was so. But of course, there was a certain amount of fear among all people. This amount of fear was not caused by any events in Kljuc. But rather by events in the overall area of the former Yugoslavia. So a certain amount of fear was transmitted to the citizens of Kljuc, and individuals or groups were mobilised on a daily basis and went to the JNA. And quite often someone who was in the JNA was killed. All this influenced the emergence of a certain amount of fear. However, I think the fear was not excessive, and people didn't think that things could happen in Kljuc the way they were happening in other parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now -- we're going chronologically in time, Mr. Kalabic. So the next document in chronological order is Document P22. Exhibit P22. And this is a document from 29 October of 1991, and it's tab 5 in your book. If you look at the second page, you'll see that it's a document allegedly sent out by Radoslav Brdjanin as a result of some meetings that took place on the 26th of October in Banja Luka. And it appears to be basically a set of instructions. I want to ask you about whether you ever remember seeing this in Kljuc, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Seen it where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing it in Kljuc, or anywhere else, this document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I personally did not have an opportunity of seeing this document in Kljuc. And I think that the president, Mr. Jovanic, did not have an opportunity of seeing it either because looking at the document, looking through it briefly, I can see that it was sent by telex. And at that time, the room where the telex was in Kljuc Municipality, there were two officers there -- two officials, rather. One was Croatian; the other was Muslim. And every document that arrived on the telex they handed first to Mr. Filipovic. And after that, he decided at his own discretion whether he would hand this document to President Banjac or not. This document did not reach President Banjac because had it done so, I and other people would probably have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is an excellent living example of how much a witness can tell you about a document that he has never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look very briefly at -- there are 14 different instructions in there. And you've had a chance to see this document when I showed it to you yesterday. And the question I have was, was there -- this document is 29 October, I believe. In that period of time, October, November, December, January, in the next three or four months, were any of the things listed in here actually implemented in Kljuc? Any of them?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: None of this was implemented in Kljuc in the period in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next document that I want you to look at refers to this one. It's P90. And it's at tab 6 in your book. And this is an official statement from the Muslim Bosniak Organisation of Kljuc and the Party of Democratic Action, Kljuc town board, just two days later, 31 October. And you'll notice in the first paragraph, it speaks about this document having been received in the Municipality of Kljuc, signed by Mr. Brdjanin, approved by Mr. Karadzic. And you'll see that this official statement from MBO says a couple of things that I want to draw your attention to. "Aware of the difficulty situation that Bosnia and Herzegovina is in, but also of the fact that the war has not echoed in our community, that Kljuc is peaceful, we hereby ask the forces acting in the spirit of these Orders whether they want the shooting to begin in Kljuc as well." And then secondly, "If they want peace, such orders should not be issued, at least not in Kljuc." Now, you've just told us that nothing in that order was implemented. What does this indicate to you with regard to what was going on between the various groups in Kljuc at that time, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Nothing was implemented in Kljuc that was mentioned in the previous document, nor could it have been, because if the document existed, it was not in the hands of President Banjac. This document, however, was used by the MBO and SDA to issue a communique which might have upset the population of the Municipality of Kljuc, the entire population. I don't remember this being published, but I assume that in circles closer to the Muslim Bosniak Organisation and the SDA, it was thoroughly analysed and that the members of those parties were fully familiar with it. This is one of the communiques that could have contributed to negative developments in interethnic relations in Kljuc Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a document, sir, at tab 27 of your book, the last document in your book. It's Exhibit P25. I've only got it there so you can refresh your memory as to what it is. It's the variant A and B document which you have seen. And I'll ask you if you've seen it before I showed it to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this document in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with that document, I want you to look now at Exhibit P865, which is tab 7 in your book. This is a document from the 6th meeting of the executive committee of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Kljuc on 23 December. If you look at agenda item number 1, Veljko Kondic says: "Veljko Kondic advised on the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Would he be referring to that document P25 that you just looked at? Is that what you think he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look, later on, Veljko Kondic says: "Today we will determine who has to do what. And at the next meeting we'll discuss why things were not done, and those who did not work will be held responsible." And then a person called Brane Vojvodic says: "I can accept all Karadzic's proposals without seeing them." And then Veljko Kondic says: "That means that all suggestions and tasks from the instructions are accepted." So basically that means, that document was basically accepted by the SDS board in Kljuc. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was accepted without a vote, to be sure. But in essence, the document was accepted as it stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look over at -- I don't know if it's the next page in your document, but further on in the document: "After the recess, Rajko Kalabic informed on the second part of the Serbian Assembly." Then Dragan Smiljanic says: "I think that the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina is being neglected and that should be worked on since everything else is utopia." Do you have any idea what he meant by saying the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina was being neglected?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan Smiljanic, in fact, said something that was true. The Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, when Kljuc was in question, was really not something that came to life in any of its segments. That is why Mr. Smiljanic said this, and I think that he was advocating an attempt to try to bring to life the idea of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina which, in the beginning, was envisioned as an economic category on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the interests of the Serbian people and all the other peoples would be protected economically because it should be noted that at that time, all resources from all the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the budget of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the funds which were mostly located in Sarajevo. In these times of conflict, while the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was falling apart, fewer and fewer funds from Sarajevo were forwarded to certain programmes in the municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina. And therefore, the standard of living in the municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina deteriorated because of the lack of funds. At one time, we even went to Banja Luka from Kljuc to ask the president of the Banja Luka municipality which was and still is financially the strongest municipality to remit to us certain funds so that old-age pensioners in Kljuc of all three ethnic groups could be paid their pensions, which were not arriving from Sarajevo. I don't remember whether we got this in Banja Luka, but we did get some funds in Gradiska for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've more than answered the question I asked. Milan Jovicic, then, says that he thinks the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc should be proclaimed at the Assembly session. And then says: "I asked that this meeting be informed about the second stage," presumably referring again to the instructions, Document P25. And you respond to that: "The first stage is the preparation for the second stage, so there is no need to introduce the second stage." I think it's clear what you're saying there. Are you saying that all we're going to do right now is prepare, but go no further? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, although I wasn't making the decision, but I suggested that, just as I've said, the first stage is only a preparation for the second stage. And as regards the Municipality of Kljuc, in my view at the time, the second stage would not have to be implemented. Of course, I'm referring to instruction that bears the number 27 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Moving forward now in time, the next document is a 29 January 1992 document. And it has been marked DB316.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I understand, Your Honour, that there is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P872 as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- It's P872 as a Prosecutors exhibit, and I didn't discover that until this morning until Ms. Korner told me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, a report of a meeting between the SDA and MBO apparently held on January 29th. And the first paragraph reads as follows: "At yesterday's session of the SDA and MBO deputies' club, the formation of a new Municipality of Bosanski Kljuc was proclaimed, which does not accept the unlawful and unconstitutional decisions of the Municipal Assembly concerning the inclusion of this municipality into the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina." And then secondly Omer Filipovic was elected the first president of this municipality and is also the deputy president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. If we then look at the very end of this document, they're talking about the creation of nine new local communes in the new Municipality of Bosanski Kljuc that have a majority Muslim population, that they will not do that demarcation right now, but that the citizens have already expressed their will about this at rallies. "It is also true that this is the first Muslim municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but its fate depends on the move of the partner, the SDS, because if there is no regionalisation on an ethnic basis, then there will be no Municipality of Bosanski Kljuc either." Were you aware of this going on at the time and what the MBO and SDA was doing in trying to set up a Bosanski Kljuc Muslim Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wish to affirm once again that at the beginning the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina was envisioned as an economic category. I will not repeat this again unless asked to explain this in greater detail. And what is stated in this exhibit confirms the earlier statements by Mr. Vinko Kondic who said that the SDA and the MBO, that is, the Muslim people, were far better organised than the Serbian people at that time in Kljuc. This material shows that with regard to the division of Kljuc Municipality into two municipalities, one Muslim and one Serb, was something that all citizens of Muslim ethnicity knew about. It also states that they agreed with this. Whether this occurred spontaneously or whether it was their response to the establishment of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina, when we assemblymen -- I was not an assemblyman, but when the municipal assembly of Kljuc reached the decision to join the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, then Serbs and Muslims alike were equally represented in that assembly. And Mr. Omer Filipovic was one of the assemblymen. Among these assemblymen, there were also assemblymen from opposition parties. Therefore, this was probably a reaction. I think that somebody from the top in Sarajevo suggested to Mr. Filipovic that he had made a mistake and that he should not accept something like that and that he would have to annul it very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just about two days later, this new Bosanski Kljuc Assembly issued a second official announcement. That's P872, and you should find it at tab 9, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Same one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It talks about failed attempts to have a meeting of the municipal assembly. It talks about representatives of the newly formed Bosanski Kljuc Municipality Assembly leaving the session of the municipal assembly. They say that "the reason for leaving the session at this time was the fact that the SDS in the joint assembly rejected their objections to the agenda that were based on a request to protect legality." They said: "These were reasoned requests by the SDA and MBO for the item on unauthorised building in Kljuc Municipality not to be removed from the agenda which was a subject of debate in earlier meetings of the executive committee at which there was mention of embezzlement and unlawful activities, and crime involving some SDS assemblymen and certain officials." Can you tell us what that was about, the unauthorised building in Kljuc Municipality, and why did that have the MBO SDA all stirred and walking out of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: At that time, on the territory of Kljuc Municipality, a building was erected, which was a commercial and artisans centre. This was the first building of this type in Kljuc. Its construction began quite a lot earlier while there was still harmony in the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, and it was the -- it was a cooperative in Kljuc that was privately owned that was doing the construction. These problems were raised as issues at the municipality only later on. I really wasn't aware that these problems existed. These issues were raised at the session of the assembly when the building was already being completed. The roof was being constructed. So I wonder why this issue was not raised earlier. And I think that this was only used as an excuse to justify walking out of the joint assembly of Kljuc Municipality by the Muslim bloc. I think it was only an excuse for them to walk out. And the real reason was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I have another question about that document after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the witness could leave, and I could just mention one matter before Your Honours leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, usher, could you escort the witness out, please. We are going to have a short break, Mr. Kalabic. 25 minutes. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take it that after one year, ten months, and however many days of trial, that Mr. Ackerman now having led from his own witness variant A and B, which was accepted, put into practice, and the allegations notwithstanding, it's now accepted that is a document issued by the SDS main board and received by the municipalities so that I no longer have to waste any further time cross-examining or calling evidence to prove it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It did occur to my mind as well actually, but of course I wouldn't have put the question myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should add, in the Rule 98, Your Honour, this particular municipality was referred to as showing it was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very clear that it was received in Kljuc, that that particular document was, and that's all I'm actually conceding at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave it at that, Ms. Korner. It doesn't lead us anywhere. We'll resume after 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we were looking at Document P872, tab 9 in your book. If you look at the very end of the document now, you'll see some more language. It indicates this second session of this Bosanski Kljuc group was held immediately after they withdrew from the municipal assembly, that they examined the situation in detail, and the move that was made was the only possible thing to do as the unruliness and lawlessness had to be finally pointed out, highlighting them now as the basis and only cause of the cessation of the work of the joint Skupstina and not political reasons which are constantly highlighted by the ranks of the SDS deceiving the public and obscuring the truth. And then finally they call on the public prosecutor's office and the competent organs of the Ministry of the Interior to conduct a thorough examination and investigation into the legality of certain decisions of the Kljuc Skupstina Opstina and certain state administrative organs and officials of the Kljuc SO. Did that investigation take place, did the public prosecutor's office conduct an investigation to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: No, the office of the public prosecutor did not carry out any investigation, although later on at the assembly, this issue was considered, this issue is illegal construction. It would be unrealistic to see the Muslim bloc leaving the joint assembly, and it says here that the only and main reason for the cessation of the work of the joint assembly is illegal construction. It also says that the political reasons do not exist. It is unrealistic, and the majority of the assemblymen would not leave the assembly only because of this suspicion about one building being erected against the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document is signed by a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: On this list, there are assemblymen of the SDA and the Muslim Bosniak Organisation. There are no other names here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the signatures at the end of that document, the tab 9 document? It's signed by a large number of people. Do you see all those signatures?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see all the signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise any of them? Do you know who any of those people are that signed it? And if so, can you tell us the names of the peoples whose signatures you can recognise.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, Omer Filipovic; Egrlic, Asim; Feho Botanic, I know them. Muhamed Filipovic; Ferid Dizdarevic; Alma Zumanovic [phoen]; Ibrahim Egrlic; Rasim Delic; Cerimagic [phoen]. I know all of these people. They were all assemblymen in the Municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were all in the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, but also apparently part of this Bosanski Kljuc Assembly also?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are the ones who signed this document as the assemblymen of the Bosanski Kljuc Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next document is DB315. It's tab 10 in your book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's also 868.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is entitled "a report from the Kljuc Municipal Assembly of 2 February 1992." It talks about events that went on in the municipal assembly a couple of days after the last document that we saw. It says at the beginning of the session, President Jovo Banjac read a statement of the SDA caucus regarding the declaration of a Muslim Municipality of Bosanski Kljuc. And the request and condition for the participation of SDA and MBO in the assembly. They wanted an item on the agenda regarding the adoption of the decision to hold a referendum on a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and a change of the decision under which the Kljuc Municipality joined the Autonomous Region of Krajina which was adopted 26 December 1991 when the assembly had been suspended. Then the response of the SDS was that the SDS caucus does not accept the request of the SDA and MBO caucus to adopt a decision on holding a referendum on an independent and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina because that's a referendum of the Muslim and Croatian ethnic communities. Since the Serbian ethnic community held its referendum in the form of a plebiscite and got an answer to the question of what the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina want. Therefore, the Serbian people will not take part in the referendum and for this reason do not need a referendum. And after this reply from the SDS, Omer Filipovic took the floor and said he was going to present the views of the SDA and MBO. And you'll see those outlined at some length, then, in this document. He says if the municipal assembly doesn't adopt a decision regarding a referendum on an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the SDA and MBO would do that and they would organise the referendum among the Muslim people and among those peoples and ethnic minorities who want that. They are calling for reformulating the decision under which Kljuc Municipality joined the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. And then he speaks about transforming local communes. Do you know what he's talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Omer Filipovic presented a condition for the work of the Muslim bloc, and that was the request for the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc to adopt a decision on holding a referendum on an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Obviously the SDS assemblymen could not accept such a thing because the plebiscite had been held amongst the Serbian people, and the Serbian people opted for the nonacceptance of such a referendum. Unfortunately, in this Assembly of the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'm sorry. The only thing I'm really interested in is if you know what he meant when he spoke about transforming local communes. I think the rest of it is pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The transformation of local communes referred to the establishment of nine local communes in which Muslims would be a majority. Those local communes would then be legalised by a decision of the municipal assembly, and this would serve to give legality to the newly established Muslim assembly of Kljuc. So this referred to the nine Muslim local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document then talks -- says: "A real storm started when the Assembly President - that would be Mr. Banjac - proposed taking off the agenda a report on the illegal construction in Kljuc Municipality with the explanation that it is incomplete and should be supplemented with concrete data. "There was a discussion that ensued. It triggered a storm immediately at the beginning. Muhamed Filipovic, Jovo Malbesa, and Asim Egrlic took part in the discussion." Egrlic disagreed with the President's explanation on postponing and asked the SDA and MBO deputies to leave, which they then apparently did. They apparently departed the assembly. Then it says for a moment, the situation became uneasy but the session continued since besides the SDS deputies' opposition, deputies... And there was a quorum for the assembly to work. Then it talks about additional discussion and lists the names of some people who took part in that discussion. Can you just tell the Chamber the people that are listed there, Milan Jovicic and that group of people, are those SDS delegates? Are they all Serbs? Tell us who they are.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Milan Jovicic and Ljuban Jovicic are SDS members. Azimir Burzic, I believe, is -- was an independent candidate who had his own party. Mirko Kvrgic was the president of Mr. Nijaz Durakovic's party of the SDP. And Jovo Dimitrovic was a member of Mr. Ante Markovic's party of reformists. Azimir Burzic, I believe that he was from a mixed marriage, and the rest of them are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in concluding this document in concluding that what --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we even get the question, the whole question is beginning to be leading. Am I correct in assuming that this document...? The proper question is: What does this document say, or whatever it is, but not am I correct in assuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, do you have any major difficulty in rephrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I have no difficulty in rephrasing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the SDA and MBO delegates there suggesting that they were not willing to go along with a majority vote on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's still leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is leading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What were the SDA delegates doing? That is the proper way of asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you don't need to explain it further. You're right, Ms. Korner. Please, don't lead. Mr. Ackerman, rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these delegates saying with regard to whether or not -- to their position regarding the vote in the assembly regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Having received information -- actually having listened to Mr. Jovo Banjac, the president of the assembly, the present assemblymen of the Muslim bloc again referred to the information on illegal construction. And they used this illegal construction to leave the session of the municipal assembly. Before that, they raised four or five very important issues on which the municipal assembly had to vote without mentioning the illegal construction. The first one was referendum. The second was autonomous region. Three, local communes. The fourth was the implementation of the laws passed by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And five concerned some issues regarding the illegal work of the municipal assembly. The Muslim bloc representatives again used illegal construction as it says in this text to leave the joint assembly. They did not use the previous issues that they raised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next meeting I want to draw your attention to is a meeting of the municipal board of the SDS, then, held on 18 February 1992. That's Document P876, your tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, I'm sorry, I gave a wrong exhibit for the last document. It's P873. I said 868, and it's 873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at item 1 on the agenda, it refers to you. It says: "Rajko Kalabic addressed the meeting underlining the importance of adoption of a constitution by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the referendum." What was that important about? What were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: At that time, we believed that it would be very important to adopt a constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because we believed that in that way, the referendum could be stopped. The referendum at which two peoples were supposed to adopt a decision on Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state. We believed that if we adopted a constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we could prevent the referendum. Unfortunately, the referendum did take place. And I've already said that the HDZ and SDS came to some joint positions in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were some joint positions that could be interpreted as something that would indicate that there wouldn't be any referendum. However, the referendum did take place without the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It then says that you spoke about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into cantons, and that you raised the issue of converging positions of the HDZ and the SDS. Is that what you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer yes or no, please. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little further down in the document, you again speak. You say: "All parties members have distanced themselves from Vinko Stupar's statements because he is not a member of the SDS. As for the division of Kljuc into cantons, it will proceed as we agree, but we shall not give up anything that is ours. We should pursue a single policy with regard to the Serbian people. The SDS thinks that what M. Babic has proposed is the best solution, only it is not practicable." Do you have any memory of what it was you were specifically referring to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the contents of the entire paragraph, or are you interested in any particular part of it, Mr. Ackerman? Because there is two parts. There is Babic, and then there is also the division. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22528 to 22537.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there are two parts in there, Your Honour, and I am interested in his memory with regard to all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one. I think I would suggest you address him straight away to the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one was distancing yourselves from the statements of Vinko Stupar. Do you remember what that was about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vinko Stupar talked about the division of the Municipality of Kljuc that was already underway. We could not support that, and that's why we have distanced ourselves from some of his statements that concerned the division of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already know that the MBO was talking about these communes that would be part of the -- Bosniak Kljuc. Is that what this discussion is about, is what communes would be Bosanski Kljuc and what communes would be basically Srpski Kljuc, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Stupar advocated such a position, which was not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was the SDS position different from Stupar's?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The SDS in Kljuc tried to preserve peace, to minimise tensions among different ethnic groups. We wanted Kljuc to remain peaceful and calm. We wanted it to continue being one municipality, and not a municipality that would be divided into two ethnically-based parts. And the SDS managed to have it that way for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any memory now about what it was that M. Babic had proposed that you characterise as the best solution but not practicable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is this Babic, first of all? Because we have heard of different Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me who Babic is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that this was Mr. Milan Babic from Knin. And about his proposal for an independent Serbian state that would be a joint state for the part in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the part in Croatia. Obviously, we believed that this would be the best thing for the Serbian people in that area, but we also believe that this was not feasible, that it was not practicable, and that's why we didn't accept that proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next part of this document, you'll see it a little further in the document. Jovanka Cvijic says: "It is a disgrace that Muslims are putting up barricades while we people are being taken in - something. Our reactions are slow." Were there any barricades being put up by people in Kljuc at this time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Not in Kljuc. There were no barricades in Kljuc at that time. I don't remember that any barricades were put up at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what this person is talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: I assume -- this is Mrs. Jovanka Cvijic who resided in a village in which there was a Muslim majority. And I suppose that she must have noticed something there and mentioned it at this session. We didn't have any significant information about that, and that's why we did not seriously consider this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look a little further through the document, you'll see that you speak again. And you say: "It will be well advised to know if the army will come by Friday or not. Politics has no place on a work site." Can you explain that statement to the Trial Chamber. What are you talking about? There are two things you say there, one about the army coming and one about politics on the work site. Take your time, and if you remember, tell the Chamber what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA was being transferred from Croatia either to Bosnia and Herzegovina or to Yugoslavia. I'm not sure. But there was an engineering regiment that was supposed to come from Croatia and be accommodated in an industrial facility which was on the border between the municipalities of Kljuc and Bosanski Petrovac. There was a lot of discussion about that, and there was a lot of stories about that which caused a certain degree of unrest among the population. And since some deadlines were mentioned and these deadlines were not met, I raised that issue at one of the meetings, and I asked whether anybody knew whether the next deadline would be met for this to happen. So that would be the first part of my answer. It was my general view that politics should not interfere with the work of economic subjects. After the disappearance of the League of Communists in this area and after the creation of the parties that were in power, all the party activities were removed from companies. And it was in that sense that I spoke at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next document is P897, and I think we can deal with this rather quickly. It's at tab 14. It's from May of 1992, but we don't know what day in May. It's called "a proposed work schedule for municipal bodies in war conditions." And several pages in, in the English, it's on the fourth page, it names an executive board, and lists you as number 6 as a member of that executive board. Is it the case that you were -- you became a member of some executive board as a result of this document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not a member, or rather I had not been nominated as a member of the executive board because this is just a proposal. This was a different man, but my name was put there by mistake under number 6. It should say "Rade," not "Rajko" as the first name. This document relied on the instructions that I have as number 27. And of course --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the document P25, the instructions for the organisation and so forth?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
